rationale: Job 9:8 says of God, "He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea" (BSB). In Swete's Septuagint the line reads peripatōn hōs ep' edaphous epi thalassēs, "walking as on ground upon the sea." Matthew uses the same verb with the same preposition: Jesus came "walking on the sea" (14:25-26, BSB; Greek peripatōn epi at 14:25, epi ... peripatounta at 14:26). The editions split on the case of the noun. At 14:25 the Byzantine and Textus Receptus editions read the genitive epi tēs thalassēs, the Septuagint's case, and SBL, Nestle 1904, Westcott-Hort and Tischendorf read the accusative epi tēn thalassan; at 14:26 the split runs the other way. Matthew gives no citation formula and does not name Job, so the type is allusion, not quotation, following conn-matt8-storm-psalm107. The label is plausible, not strong. Alexander MacLaren quotes the Septuagint of Job 9:8 on this scene ("He walketh on the sea as on a pavement") and calls the walk "a revelation of divine power." Richard Hays argues for a Job 9 echo in Mark's version, as reported by Derek Rishmawy and Andrew Perriman. Rishmawy summarizes two lines of evidence. One, the shared Greek wording with the Septuagint, holds for Matthew too. The other, Mark's clause "He intended to pass by them" (Mark 6:48) beside Job 9:11, "Were He to pass by me" (BSB), does not, because Matthew does not have that clause. Perriman, who doubts most of Hays's divine-identity readings, says this argument "does not seem too far-fetched, at least when taken in isolation," though he ends by leaning toward an exodus background instead (see conn-matt14-path-psalm77). No source read for this lesson argues the link for Matthew's wording in particular.
